name: TaskRunner
title: Task Runner
description: Runs one task a step at a time, handing out what it still needs and taking back the answers
whenToUse: Carry a task that is waiting on a person through to the end: an application half filled in, a form left at a step, anything held open for someone with some of it already answered. Give it the task and what is already known, and it answers with the one step still outstanding and the fields that step asks for, takes the answers back, and says when nothing is left. Deciding WHICH task to do, and asking the questions out loud, are different jobs: this one only works out what is still needed and keeps count as it comes in. It walks the steps in the order the task declares them, so a later step is never handed out while an earlier one is short.

inputs.name: collected
inputs.description: Answers just given, as { field: value }

outputs.name: task
outputs.description: The task as it stands now

runId.title: The task
runId.description: The paused task's run id. Upstream data works here, which is how one workflow carries a different person's task each time it is called.

startAgain.title: Clear these fields and ask again
startAgain.description: TESTING ONLY. Field names separated by commas. Those answers are erased on the real record and asked for again; everything else, including the product, is left as it is. This cannot be undone. Leave blank.

followUpField.title: Field holding when to come back
followUpField.description: When this field has a value, the task waits until then rather than for the person to return. It must be a full date and time. Blank means nothing schedules it.

keepForDays.title: Keep an unfinished task for
keepForDays.description: Days a half finished task is kept before it expires.

completeWhenDone.title: Complete the task when nothing is outstanding
completeWhenDone.description: Off leaves the task open with everything filled in, for whoever may take the last step. On marks it finished.

authRequired.title: Require sign-in
authRequired.description: Only a signed-in caller may run this step. Leave off and it runs for whoever the workflow's trigger admitted, which is the usual answer.

authRole.title: Require role
authRole.description: A claim the caller's account must carry, as noun:verb (finance:approve, payments:refund). Leave blank to require only that they are signed in.

package.name: flow
package.packageFile:
# FLOW AS MANIFESTS, node by node.
#
# The one package that can migrate INCREMENTALLY, because it declares no credentials. The
# all-or-nothing rule that forced `aws-toolkit` and `cloudinary` to be split came entirely from
# the credential coexistence check (a node needs `credentials/<name>.yaml` in its own package,
# but that file alongside a code `registerCredential` is an error). With no credentials there is
# no conflict, and `src/index.ts` registers each node on its own line — so a node moves by
# writing its manifest and deleting those two lines.
#
# ONE HOST, AND ONLY THE PLATFORM'S OWN. For most of this package's life the list was empty,
# and that was not an omission: nothing here reached the network at all. TaskRunner is the
# exception and a narrow one. A task's half finished state is the platform's own record, kept
# as a paused run, so reading and writing it is a loopback call to the engine and never a
# vendor. The spatial package carries the same single entry for the same reason.
#
# The numeric form deliberately: the pattern rejects a bare "localhost", and the engine's
# address is built as `http://127.0.0.1:${ENGINE_PORT ?? 4101}` by the executor itself, so
# nothing here chooses the host. A wildcard would turn a flow package into a way to send a
# person's half written application somewhere else.
#
# WHAT IS STILL CODE, and why:
#
#   UMAP  runs umap-js IN PROCESS. Genuine local compute, reaching no host. Also of doubtful
#         value as written: it received ONE vector, faked a second by copying it with +0.0001
#         on every element so umap-js would run, and returned near-meaningless coordinates —
#         the real reduction lives in services/umap now. A candidate for removal, undecided.
#
#   SendObject  RETIRED to _legacy, user decision 2026-07-29 — it published to the live
#               session rather than answering the graph, and the `publish` capability that
#               replaced that lane (see Suggestions) covers the need.
#
# Suggestions, which used to sit on this list for the same reason as SendObject, is now a
# manifest: what actually needed code was one push into the caller's template state, and that
# is the executor's `publish` capability (api/publish.yaml) — declared under `requires` below.
#
# AND ONE REMOVAL rather than a migration. Gone from the catalog, so a saved workflow naming
# it now fails to resolve the type:
#
#   MCP             a generic schema-driven mcpService provider from before real service nodes
#                   existed. Superseded by UnoverseMCP in the engine and by per-vendor providers
#                   (HubspotMCP, SalesforceMCP, SlackMCP), so nothing needed it.
#
# FieldValidator was on this list, removed because its five outputs all derive from one
# properties-map cascade and expressions had no way to bind an intermediate value — the cascade
# had to be written out again inside every expression needing it; `completionPercentage` alone
# came to four copies. Named helpers (shared/helpers.yaml) are exactly that binding, so it is
# BACK, same type and connectors, and any workflow that named it resolves again.

name: flow
displayName: Flow
description: Control flow, routing and workflow annotation
version: 2.0.0
category: flow

allowedHosts:
  - 127.0.0.1
logoUrl: https://res.cloudinary.com/sonik/image/upload/v1751366180/gravity/icons/gravityIcon.png

features:
  - Notes and documentation on the canvas
  - Branch, relay and read the running workflow's own context
  - Transform data inline, with optional content ids and run-scoped saved values
  - Loop over an array, running real workflow steps once per item
  - Validate collected data against a schema and get the next missing field to ask for
  - Walk a task's steps, handing out what is still outstanding and taking the answers back
  - Push suggested FAQs, actions and recommendations to the live chat UI

requires:
  # 1.7.0 for named helpers (shared/helpers.yaml), which FieldValidator's emit rows call —
  # the same floor spatial set when helpers landed. Previously 1.5.0.
  executorVersion: ">=1.7.0"
  # TaskRunner's three calls to the engine. Declared for the same reason as everything else
  # here: the package says which capabilities its nodes need, so an install against an
  # executor without them fails at install rather than at run.
  transport: [json]
  # Code's "Save to Context" toggle. Declared even though it cannot silently no-op the way a cache
  # read can — an executor without `save` throws rather than shrugging — because the reason to
  # declare is the same either way: the package says which platform capabilities its nodes need, so
  # installing it against an older executor fails at install rather than at run.
  state:
    - save
  # The LoopStart/LoopEnd pair. More is at stake in declaring these than in most capabilities: an
  # executor that cannot keep an index does not iterate, so an install that skipped this check would
  # run a loop body exactly once and report success.
  loop:
    - open
    - read
    - advance
  # Suggestions' whole job. Declared because on an executor without the publish lane the node
  # would emit its connector and never reach the screen — "worked" everywhere except the one
  # place it matters.
  publish: true

shared.helpers.yaml:
# FLOW'S NAMED FUNCTIONS. FieldValidator's schema cascade and Suggestions' normalizer,
# because both nodes' whole job is shaping one object that several expressions then read.
#
# FieldValidator exists again BECAUSE of this file: it was retired rather than migrated when
# every one of its five outputs derived from the same properties-map cascade and, with no way
# to bind an intermediate value, the cascade had to be written out again inside every
# expression needing it — completionPercentage alone came to four copies. Named helpers are
# the capability that reversed that decision: the cascade runs here, once, and each emit row
# picks one field.
#
# A helper sees only its arguments and its siblings: no config, no credentials, no caller
# scope. Same sandbox as every other expression, no extra authority.

helpers:
  # WHERE THE FIELDS LIVE, across the three shapes the retired node accepted — transcribed
  # from its extractSchemaInfo, cases in the same order:
  #
  #   1. a minted TOOL schema      { inputSchema: { json: { properties, required } } }
  #   2. plain JSON Schema         { properties, required }
  #   3. a bare object             its keys ARE the fields, nothing is required
  #
  # All three still arrive in practice, because the schema is whatever the upstream wire
  # carries: an agent's tool definition, an authored form schema, or a hand-built object.
  schemaInfo:
    args: [schema]
    body: >-
      return (!schema || typeof schema !== 'object')
        ? { fieldNames: [], requiredList: [], propertiesMap: {} }
        : (((schema.inputSchema || {}).json || {}).properties
            ? { fieldNames: Object.keys(schema.inputSchema.json.properties),
                requiredList: schema.inputSchema.json.required || [],
                propertiesMap: schema.inputSchema.json.properties }
            : (schema.properties
                ? { fieldNames: Object.keys(schema.properties),
                    requiredList: schema.required || [],
                    propertiesMap: schema.properties }
                : { fieldNames: Object.keys(schema), requiredList: [], propertiesMap: schema }))

  # A field is MISSING when absent, null, or the empty string — the empty string because these
  # values come off forms and chat slots, where "" is what an unanswered question produces.
  # No data at all means everything is missing, not an error: the first turn of a slot-filling
  # conversation legitimately starts from nothing.
  missingFields:
    args: [fieldNames, data]
    body: >-
      return (!data || typeof data !== 'object')
        ? fieldNames
        : fieldNames.filter(f => data[f] == null || data[f] === '')

  # THE SUGGESTIONS OBJECT, normalized at the source — transcribed from the retired
  # Suggestions executor. The template's contract is `{ text }` (the SDK stores producer data
  # opaquely and knows no "faq", UNOVERSE_STATE_MODEL §8), while authors write a string,
  # `{ text }` or `{ question }` — so the flattening happens HERE and the SDK never has to.
  #
  # Per-key fallback, signal over config, exactly as the retired node resolved it: a workflow
  # usually wires the whole object off an upstream extractor, and static config is the
  # standing default for whichever keys the signal does not carry.
  #
  # The retired node's two-level "source node / output handle" probing is deliberately NOT
  # transcribed: that unwrapped the LEGACY engine's signal envelope, and the manifest executor
  # binds the payload by input port name instead — there is nothing left to unwrap.
  suggestionsOf:
    args: [given, authored]
    body: >-
      return ((sig) => ({
        faqs: ((sig.faqs || authored.faqs) || []).map(f => ({
          text: typeof f === 'string'
            ? f
            : ((f || {}).text != null ? f.text : ((f || {}).question != null ? f.question : ''))
        })),
        actions: (sig.actions || authored.actions) || [],
        recommendations: (sig.recommendations || authored.recommendations) || []
      }))(given || {})

  # ONE report with everything the node emits. `null` rather than `undefined` for an absent
  # next field, so the emit rows can test it with a plain comparison.
  #
  # NEXT-FIELD PRIORITY is the retired node's: first missing field that the schema marks
  # required, else first missing field in schema order — `filter(...)[0] || missing[0]`
  # collapses both cases because an empty filter yields undefined and falls through.
  fieldReport:
    args: [schema, data]
    body: >-
      return ((info) =>
        ((missing) =>
          ((next) => ({
            nextField: next,
            nextFieldSchema: (next == null || info.propertiesMap[next] == null)
              ? null
              : info.propertiesMap[next],
            missingFields: missing,
            isComplete: missing.length === 0,
            completionPercentage: info.fieldNames.length === 0
              ? 100
              : Math.round((info.fieldNames.length - missing.length) / info.fieldNames.length * 100)
          }))(missing.length === 0
            ? null
            : (missing.filter(f => info.requiredList.includes(f))[0] || missing[0]))
        )(helpers.missingFields(info.fieldNames, data))
      )(helpers.schemaInfo(schema))

  # ── A TASK'S NEXT STEP ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # Beside the schema helpers above and for the same reason: two places ask the same question
  # of one task, so the arithmetic lives once. FieldValidator answers "which field is missing
  # from this schema"; these answer "which STEP of this task is still short", and a task
  # declares its own steps rather than being handed a schema.
  # A FIELD MAY BE A NAME OR A DECLARATION. A task that says `["national_id"]` and one that
  # says `[{ name: "national_id", ask: "..." }]` mean the same thing, and every caller here
  # wants the name, so the shape is flattened once.
  fieldName:
    args: [field]
    body: >-
      return typeof field === 'string'
        ? field
        : String((field || {}).name || (field || {}).field || (field || {}).key || '')

  # HELD MEANS ANSWERED. Null, undefined and the empty string are all "not yet", which is the
  # component's own rule: an empty field is correct, a guessed one is a defect. `false` and
  # `0` ARE answers, which is why this is not a truthiness test.
  isHeld:
    args: [state, name]
    body: >-
      return !!name && (state || {})[name] !== undefined
        && (state || {})[name] !== null && (state || {})[name] !== ''

  # EVERY STEP, IN ORDER, whatever shape the task declared. A task with steps keeps them; a
  # task with a flat list of fields becomes one unnamed step, so the rest of this file never
  # has to ask which kind it was handed.
  steps:
    args: [task]
    body: >-
      return (() => {
        const t = task || {};
        if (Array.isArray(t.steps) && t.steps.length) {
          return t.steps.map((s, i) => ({
            step: String((s || {}).step || (s || {}).name || (s || {}).state || ('step ' + (i + 1))),
            fields: Array.isArray((s || {}).fields) ? s.fields : []
          }));
        }
        return Array.isArray(t.fields) && t.fields.length
          ? [{ step: '', fields: t.fields }]
          : [];
      })()

  # WHAT WE NOW HOLD. The saved state is the floor and the answers just given are laid over
  # it, so a correction replaces rather than duplicates, and a field nobody mentioned keeps
  # the value it already had.
  merged:
    args: [saved, collected]
    body: >-
      return Object.assign({}, saved || {}, collected || {})

  # THE ONE STEP TO ASK FOR NOW: the first that is not finished. Null when the task is done,
  # which is the whole completion test and the reason it is not written twice.
  #
  # Steps are walked in the order the task declared them, so a task cannot be answered out of
  # order and a later step cannot be handed out while an earlier one is still short.
  # THE TASK, DUG OUT OF WHATEVER ARRIVED. A wired input does not come in bare: it arrives
  # nested by source node and output handle, `{ inputtrigger2: { output: … } }`, and a trigger
  # that was handed JSON hands it on as a STRING under `message`. Both are the platform's
  # envelope rather than anyone's data, so unwrapping belongs here and not in every caller.
  #
  # PEELED TO A FIXED DEPTH, never recursively: the sandbox has no way to define a function
  # that calls itself. Two levels covers the envelope, which is all there ever is.
  #
  # A level is "the task itself" the moment it names steps or a ref, so a task that happens to
  # arrive bare is passed straight through and nothing is peeled off it by mistake.
  taskOf:
    args: [arrived]
    body: >-
      return (() => {
        const isTask = (v) => !!v && typeof v === 'object' && (v.ref || v.steps || v.state);
        const down = (v) => (isTask(v) || !v || typeof v !== 'object') ? v : (Object.values(v)[0]);
        const found = down(down(isTask(arrived) ? arrived : arrived));
        const here = (found && typeof found === 'object') ? found : {};
        const text = typeof here.message === 'string' ? here.message.trim() : '';
        const parsed = (text.charAt(0) === '{' ? JSON.parse(text) : here);
        return (parsed && parsed.task) ? parsed.task : (parsed || {});
      })()

  # THE ONE STEP TO ASK FOR NOW: the first that is not finished. Null when the task is done,
  # which is the whole completion test and the reason it is not written twice.
  #
  # Steps are walked in the order the task declared them, so a task cannot be answered out of
  # order and a later step cannot be handed out while an earlier one is still short.
  #
  # NO LOOP, because the sandbox refuses one (`disallowed expression: ForStatement`, caught on
  # the first real run). Marking every step and taking the first short one says the same thing.
  # THE TASK'S OWN QUESTIONS, TAKEN FROM ITS STATE, for a task that declares no steps.
  #
  # EVERY question, answered or not: `nextStep` does the splitting, so what comes back here is
  # the step's whole field list. Filtering to the outstanding ones HERE instead left `held`
  # permanently empty, because there was nothing held left in the list for it to find.
  #
  # A component task's saved state IS its props slice (mcp/dataPlane.ts saves `state: props`),
  # so every field the form asks for is already a key in it: the ones answered carry a value
  # and the ones outstanding are empty. That makes the list of questions a property of the
  # record itself, and nothing has to be told twice.
  #
  # THE `Source` TWINS ARE NOT QUESTIONS. Every proposed field on a SAB application carries a
  # `<field>Source` beside it, the chip saying where the value came from. Asking someone for
  # their "national id source" is nonsense, so a key whose name ends in Source is skipped, and
  # it is written back beside the answer rather than collected.
  fromState:
    args: [state]
    body: >-
      return Object.keys(state || {})
        .filter(k => k.slice(-6) !== 'Source')

  # THE ONE STEP TO ASK FOR NOW: the first that is not finished. Null when the task is done,
  # which is the whole completion test and the reason it is not written twice.
  #
  # TWO WAYS A TASK SAYS WHAT IT WANTS, and the second needs nobody to have declared anything.
  # A task that names its steps is walked in that order, so it cannot be answered out of order
  # and a later step is never handed out while an earlier one is short. A task that names none
  # falls back to its own saved state, where an empty key is a question outstanding, and the
  # whole lot comes back as one step.
  #
  # NO LOOP, because the sandbox refuses one (`disallowed expression: ForStatement`, caught on
  # the first real run). Marking every step and taking the first short one says the same thing.
  # THE ANSWERS, WHATEVER SHAPE THEY ARRIVED IN.
  #
  # A voice that can call tools hands over ONE field at a time, named and typed:
  # `{ call: 'record_field', arguments: { field: 'monthly_income', value: '8000' } }`. Anything
  # else hands over a plain map. Both mean the same thing here, so both are turned into one.
  #
  # Peeled first, because a wired input arrives nested by source node and output handle.
  #
  # A NAMED FIELD WINS OVER A MAP. A tool call carries `field` and `value` as its arguments, so
  # reading its `arguments` as a map would write `{ field: 'monthly_income' }` into the record:
  # the NAME of the question stored as an answer, under a key nothing asked for.
  answersOf:
    args: [arrived]
    body: >-
      return (() => {
        const bare = (v) => (!v || typeof v !== 'object') ? {} : v;
        const named = (v) => bare(v).arguments || bare(v).answers || bare(v).field || bare(v).call;
        const lvl = (v) => named(v) ? v : Object.values(bare(v))[0];
        const here = bare(lvl(lvl(arrived)));
        const args = bare(here.arguments || here);

        // MANY AT ONCE, which is how a call that kept its answers in its head hands them back.
        // Every pause in a conversation is a hand-off, so the voice collects everything and
        // gives it all up at the end: `answers` is that list.
        if (Array.isArray(args.answers)) {
          return args.answers
            .filter(a => a && typeof a.field === 'string' && a.field)
            .reduce((acc, a) => Object.assign(acc, { [a.field]: a.value }), {});
        }

        // ONE, named. A tool call carries `field` and `value` as its arguments, so reading them
        // as a map would store the NAME of the question as an answer, under a key nothing asked
        // for. The named field wins.
        // NOTHING ELSE IS AN ANSWER. Anything that is not a list of `answers` or one named
        // `field` is some other shape entirely, and handing it back whole writes ITS keys into
        // the record as though a person had said them. Measured 2026-09-22: a delegation
        // hand-off put `id`, `request` and an entire call transcript into a customer's credit
        // card application, and they survived every reset because a reset only empties the
        // fields it was told to. An empty result is correct here: it means this pass collected
        // nothing, which is a thing that happens.
        return (typeof args.field === 'string' && args.field)
          ? { [args.field]: args.value }
          : {};
      })()

  # THE STATE THIS PASS WORKS FROM, and the one place the reset happens.
  #
  # Ordinarily it is what the record holds. With `startAgain` on it is the same KEYS with every
  # value emptied, which is what "back to the first step" means for a task whose questions are
  # its own state: keep the list, lose the answers. Dropping the keys instead would leave the
  # node with nothing to ask for at all.
  #
  # Written as one helper because three places need the same answer: the events table, the call
  # that saves, and the test for whether anything is outstanding.
  # THE STATE THIS PASS WORKS FROM, and the one place a reset happens.
  #
  # Ordinarily it is what the record holds. When fields are named to clear, those keys are
  # emptied and EVERYTHING ELSE IS LEFT ALONE: a task's state carries what the call is asking
  # for and also what the task arrived with, the product, their name, their email, and wiping
  # the second kind leaves a call that cannot say what it is ringing about.
  #
  # The keys are kept and emptied rather than removed, because for a task whose questions are
  # its own state the key IS the question. Dropping it would leave nothing to ask.
  # WHICH FIELDS THIS PASS IS ALLOWED TO WIPE, and the answer is none of them once the
  # conversation has started. `startAgain` is a testing lever: it puts a task back to its first
  # question. Applied on EVERY pass it does the opposite of what it says, because a pass that
  # carries answers reads the record fresh, blanks it, and writes only what arrived — so the
  # answer given two questions ago is gone. It wipes on the way in and never again.
  clearing:
    args: [collected, startAgain]
    body: >-
      return collected && Object.keys(collected).length ? '' : String(startAgain || '')

  baseState:
    args: [saved, clear]
    body: >-
      return (() => {
        const names = String(clear || '').split(',').map(s => s.trim()).filter(s => s);
        const held = saved || {};
        return names.length
          ? names.reduce((acc, k) => Object.assign(acc, { [k]: '' }), Object.assign({}, held))
          : held;
      })()

  nextStep:
    args: [task, state]
    body: >-
      return (() => {
        const declared = helpers.steps(task);
        const all = declared.length
          ? declared
          : [{ step: '', fields: helpers.fromState(state) }];
        const marked = all.map((s, i) => ({
          step: s.step,
          stepNumber: i + 1,
          stepsTotal: all.length,
          fields: s.fields.filter(f => !helpers.isHeld(state, helpers.fieldName(f))),
          // WHAT WE HOLD, WITH THE VALUES, not just the names. A name alone tells whoever is
          // asking that a field is answered but not what it says, so a call knew it had the
          // product's title and could not name the product: "your application" instead of
          // "your AQSAT Credit Card application". The values are the person's own and the
          // caller is already speaking to them, so there is nothing here they may not hear.
          held: s.fields.filter(f => helpers.isHeld(state, helpers.fieldName(f)))
                        .reduce((acc, f) => Object.assign(acc, {
                          [helpers.fieldName(f)]: state[helpers.fieldName(f)]
                        }), {})
        }));
        const short = marked.filter(m => m.fields.length > 0);
        return short.length
          ? Object.assign({}, short[0], { outstandingCount: short[0].fields.length })
          : null;
      })()

files.api/events.yaml:
# ONE QUESTION, ASKED BY EVERY ROW: what does this task still need, given everything now held.
# Recomputing it per row is deliberate, exactly as FieldValidator does it: the answer is a pure
# function of the task and the state, and rows cannot share a binding.
#
# THE STATE IS THE SAVED ROW WITH THE NEW ANSWERS LAID OVER IT, here and in run.yaml both, and
# the order is the point: a correction replaces, and a field nobody mentioned keeps what it had.
#
# WHAT THE TASK WANTS comes from the state as well, when nothing declared steps: a component
# task's slice holds every field the form asks for, so an empty key IS an outstanding question.
# `helpers.nextStep` falls back to that on its own, which is why nothing here passes a schema.
#
# `task` AND `done` ARE EACH OTHER'S OPPOSITE. While a step is short there is something
# to ask and the task is not finished; the moment nextStep comes back null there is nothing to
# ask and it is. Two gated rows rather than one row carrying a flag, so nothing downstream has
# to test a field before acting: a connector that fires IS the instruction.

- emit: task
  when: >-
    return helpers.nextStep(helpers.taskOf(signal.signal),
      helpers.merged(helpers.baseState(((calls.saved || {}).paused || {}).state, helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain)), helpers.answersOf(signal.collected))) !== null
  value: >-
    return helpers.nextStep(helpers.taskOf(signal.signal),
      helpers.merged(helpers.baseState(((calls.saved || {}).paused || {}).state, helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain)), helpers.answersOf(signal.collected)))

- emit: done
  when: >-
    return helpers.nextStep(helpers.taskOf(signal.signal),
      helpers.merged(helpers.baseState(((calls.saved || {}).paused || {}).state, helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain)), helpers.answersOf(signal.collected))) === null
  value: "return true"
files.api/run.yaml:
# FOUR CALLS, ALL TO THE PLATFORM'S OWN ENGINE, and each one guarded so exactly the ones that
# apply run. A task IS a run (migration 056): a component task half filled in is a run of one
# node paused at the person, one row per owner and task, the values encrypted, saved again at
# every step and cleared when it finishes.
#
# SO THE NODE IS TOLD ONE THING, the row's id, and asks the row for the rest. Which component
# it is, whose it is and which workflow it belongs to are all columns; making a caller pass
# them alongside would be asking them to repeat the record and to be right about it.
#
# NO CREDENTIAL, and that is not an oversight. The engine's listener is never published or
# proxied, so a node calling it is already inside the trust boundary (package.yaml, and the
# reasoning the spatial package sets out at length).

- name: run
  # THE ROW ITSELF. It answers who and what; it cannot answer WITH WHAT, because the state is
  # encrypted at rest and this route hands the column over as it is stored. That is the whole
  # reason there is a second call below rather than one.
  #
  # THE ID, FROM THE CONFIG OR OUT OF WHAT ARRIVED. The config field is the ordinary way and an
  # author templates it from upstream. The fallback is not politeness: a trigger fired by hand
  # carries its whole input as a JSON STRING under `message`, so the template resolves to
  # nothing and the URL becomes `/executions/` — a 404 that reads like a missing route rather
  # than a missing id. `taskOf` already knows how to peel that, so it peels this too.
  method: GET
  url: >-
    return scope.engineUrl + '/executions/' + encodeURIComponent(
      String(config.runId || helpers.taskOf(signal.signal).runId || '').trim())
  transport: json
  timeoutMs: 15000
  error:
    when: "return !response || !!response.error || !response.task_ref"
    message: >-
      return 'no paused task at ' + String(config.runId || '') + ': '
        + JSON.stringify(response || {}).slice(0, 200)

- name: saved
  # WHAT IS ALREADY HELD, decrypted by the route that owns the key, and read fresh every pass
  # rather than carried in a variable. On the first pass it is what an earlier conversation
  # left behind; on a later one it is what the pass before this one wrote. Reading it back
  # makes the node self correcting: if a write failed, the next pass sees the field is still
  # outstanding and asks again instead of believing its own memory.
  method: GET
  url: >-
    return scope.engineUrl + '/runs/paused'
      + '?workflowId=' + encodeURIComponent(String(calls.run.workflow_id || ''))
      + '&userId=' + encodeURIComponent(String(calls.run.user_id || ''))
      + '&taskRef=' + encodeURIComponent(String(calls.run.task_ref || ''))
  transport: json
  timeoutMs: 15000
  error:
    when: "return !response || !!response.error"
    message: "return 'runs/paused failed: ' + JSON.stringify(response || {}).slice(0, 300)"

- name: reset
  # THE WIPE ITSELF, and it has to be written down or it is not a reset: every pass reads the
  # record fresh, so blanking the state only in memory would ask for everything once and then
  # find it all filled in again on the next answer.
  #
  # ON THE WAY IN AND NEVER AGAIN — that is what `helpers.clearing` is for. A pass carrying
  # answers must not wipe, or the record it reads fresh is blanked and rewritten with only what
  # arrived just now, and the answer given two questions ago is gone. Written the obvious way
  # this lever quietly destroys the conversation it was meant to restart.
  when: "return String(helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain) || '').trim() !== ''"
  method: POST
  url: "return scope.engineUrl + '/runs/pause'"
  transport: json
  timeoutMs: 15000
  body:
    workflowId: "return String(calls.run.workflow_id || '')"
    userId: "return String(calls.run.user_id || '')"
    taskRef: "return String(calls.run.task_ref || '')"
    state: >-
      return helpers.baseState(((calls.saved || {}).paused || {}).state, helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain))
    wake: "return 'reply'"
    # `Date.iso`, NOT `new Date(...)`: the expression sandbox refuses a NewExpression and names
    # this exact case, so the constructor fails at run time rather than at lint.
    expiresAt: >-
      return Date.iso(Date.now()
        + (config.keepForDays != null ? Number(config.keepForDays) : 14) * 86400000)
  error:
    when: "return !response || !!response.error || !response.executionId"
    message: "return 'runs/pause (start again) failed: ' + JSON.stringify(response || {}).slice(0, 300)"

- name: record
  # ONLY WHEN SOMETHING WAS JUST GIVEN. A pass that merely asks the next question writes
  # nothing, so the expiry is not pushed out by a call where the person said nothing, and the
  # row is not rewritten with what it already holds.
  when: "return !!signal.collected && Object.keys(helpers.answersOf(signal.collected)).length > 0"
  method: POST
  url: "return scope.engineUrl + '/runs/pause'"
  transport: json
  timeoutMs: 15000
  body:
    workflowId: "return String(calls.run.workflow_id || '')"
    userId: "return String(calls.run.user_id || '')"
    taskRef: "return String(calls.run.task_ref || '')"
    # THE WHOLE STATE, NEVER A PATCH. The route replaces what it is given, so sending only the
    # new answers would drop every earlier one. The merge is the helper's, so the state written
    # here and the state emitted on the connector are one object computed one way.
    state: "return helpers.merged(helpers.baseState(((calls.saved || {}).paused || {}).state, helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain)), helpers.answersOf(signal.collected))"
    # WHAT WAKES IT, and the person decides which.
    #
    # `reply` is the ordinary case: this task is carried by a conversation, so what resumes it
    # is them answering, not them opening a page.
    #
    # `timer` the moment they named a time. "Ring me Thursday" is a real answer and the row can
    # hold it, so a declined call becomes a scheduled one rather than a task nobody returns to.
    wake: >-
      return String(helpers.merged(
        helpers.baseState(((calls.saved || {}).paused || {}).state, helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain)),
        helpers.answersOf(signal.collected)
      )[String(config.followUpField || '')] || '').trim() ? 'timer' : 'reply'

    # WHEN, and only when a time was actually given: the route keeps whatever it is sent, so a
    # blank here must be ABSENT rather than an empty string that parses to nothing.
    wakeAt: >-
      return String(helpers.merged(
        helpers.baseState(((calls.saved || {}).paused || {}).state, helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain)),
        helpers.answersOf(signal.collected)
      )[String(config.followUpField || '')] || '').trim() || undefined
    # `Date.iso`, NOT `new Date(...)`: the expression sandbox refuses a NewExpression and names
    # this exact case, so the constructor fails at run time rather than at lint.
    expiresAt: >-
      return Date.iso(Date.now()
        + (config.keepForDays != null ? Number(config.keepForDays) : 14) * 86400000)
  error:
    when: "return !response || !!response.error || !response.executionId"
    message: "return 'runs/pause failed: ' + JSON.stringify(response || {}).slice(0, 300)"

- name: finish
  # NOTHING OUTSTANDING, AND FINISHING IS OURS TO DO. Both halves matter: an application only
  # the customer may submit is filled to the end and deliberately left open, and the toggle is
  # how an author says so. The completion test is helpers.nextStep returning null, the same
  # test the `done` connector fires on, written once.
  when: >-
    return config.completeWhenDone !== false
      && helpers.nextStep(
           helpers.taskOf(signal.signal),
           helpers.merged(helpers.baseState(((calls.saved || {}).paused || {}).state, helpers.clearing(signal.collected, config.startAgain)), helpers.answersOf(signal.collected))
         ) === null
  method: POST
  url: "return scope.engineUrl + '/runs/complete'"
  transport: json
  timeoutMs: 15000
  body:
    workflowId: "return String(calls.run.workflow_id || '')"
    userId: "return String(calls.run.user_id || '')"
    taskRef: "return String(calls.run.task_ref || '')"
  error:
    when: "return !response || !!response.error"
    message: "return 'runs/complete failed: ' + JSON.stringify(response || {}).slice(0, 300)"
files.config.yaml:
configSchema:
  type: object
  required: [runId]
  properties:
    # THE ONE THING THIS NODE IS TOLD. A paused task is a row, and the row already holds which
    # component it is, whose it is and what is filled in, so naming the row names all of it.
    # Passing the ref and the owner alongside would be asking a caller to repeat what the
    # record already says, and to be right about it.
    #
    # A CONFIG FIELD RATHER THAN A CONNECTOR, the same choice SpatialDetail makes with its
    # universal id: the engine resolves the template before the node runs, so the node fires
    # once already holding everything it needs.
    runId:
      type: string
      title: The task
      description: >-
        The paused task's run id. Upstream data works here, which is how one workflow carries
        a different person's task each time it is called.
      default: ""
      ui:field: template

    # CLEAR THESE AND ASK FOR THEM AGAIN. FOR TESTING, and the description says so in the
    # panel because nothing else will: this EMPTIES those answers on the person's real record
    # the moment the node runs. It is not a dry run and there is no undo.
    #
    # NAMED, NOT ALL. A task's state holds two different kinds of thing: what the call is
    # asking for, and what the task ARRIVED with — the product being applied for, their name,
    # their email. Wiping both leaves a call that cannot say what it is ringing about, which
    # is a worse test than no test. The node cannot tell the two apart, so rather than guess
    # it asks: name the ones to clear and everything else is left alone.
    #
    # Blank, the normal case, resets nothing.
    startAgain:
      type: string
      title: Clear these fields and ask again
      description: >-
        TESTING ONLY. Field names separated by commas. Those answers are erased on the real
        record and asked for again; everything else, including the product, is left as it is.
        This cannot be undone. Leave blank.
      default: ""
      ui:field: template

    # WHEN TO COME BACK TO IT, if the person said.
    #
    # A paused task already knows how to wait for a clock: the row carries `wake` and `wake_at`
    # (migration 056), and `timer` is one of the three things that can wake it. Nothing was
    # setting them, so every task waited for the person to come back rather than for us to.
    #
    # THE FIELD, NOT THE VALUE. Which field carries a follow-up time is the TASK's business,
    # not this node's: a call collects a callback time, a form might collect a renewal date.
    # Name it here, and whenever it has a value the task wakes then instead of waiting to be
    # opened. Its value must be a full timestamp, because "Thursday morning" is not a time
    # until something has decided which Thursday.
    followUpField:
      type: string
      title: Field holding when to come back
      description: >-
        When this field has a value, the task waits until then rather than for the person to
        return. It must be a full date and time. Blank means nothing schedules it.
      default: callback_at
      ui:field: template

    # HOW LONG A HALF FINISHED TASK IS KEPT. It is saved again at every step, so this counts
    # from the last thing they told us, never from when the task began.
    keepForDays:
      type: number
      title: Keep an unfinished task for
      description: Days a half finished task is kept before it expires.
      default: 14
      minimum: 1
      maximum: 365

    # FINISHING IS A SEPARATE PERMISSION FROM FILLING IN, and the reason is a real one rather
    # than caution: a task whose last act is not ours to take, an application only the customer
    # may submit, is filled to the end and LEFT there. That is a complete run, not a failed one,
    # and the toggle is how an author says which kind of task this is.
    completeWhenDone:
      type: boolean
      title: Complete the task when nothing is outstanding
      description: >-
        Off leaves the task open with everything filled in, for whoever may take the last step.
        On marks it finished.
      default: true
      ui:widget: toggle

  ui:order: [runId, keepForDays, completeWhenDone, startAgain]
files.interface.yaml:
inputs:
  # STARTS IT. The task's run id is a config field templated from whatever is upstream, so the
  # node fires once already holding everything it needs (signal-routing.md, "Two inputs never
  # arrive together").
  - name: signal
    type: object
    description: What starts it
    required: false

  # THE ANSWERS COMING BACK, while the conversation is still going. `CONTINUE` is what makes
  # that possible: the value is handed to the step already running rather than starting the
  # node again, which would hand out the same step afresh.
  #
  # WIRE THE FINAL ANSWERS, NEVER A STREAM. A stream sends what it has so far on every change,
  # so a half heard number would be written to the record and then written again.
  - name: collected
    type: object
    signal: CONTINUE
    description: "Answers just given, as { field: value }"
    required: false

outputs:
  # THE TASK AS IT STANDS, and the only thing anything downstream needs: which step, what is
  # still outstanding, the values already held, and how far through it is. One object, read
  # whichever part you want.
  #
  # ONE STEP AT A TIME on purpose: whatever is asking can hold one short list in its head, and
  # cannot wander into a later step or decide it has finished early.
  #
  # There was a second output carrying the whole state. It went: the state is already in here,
  # and a slice of one object is not a second idea.
  - name: task
    type: object
    description: The task as it stands now

  # SETTLES THE NODE. Nothing outstanding, the task completed, and the run moves on.
  - name: done
    type: boolean
    description: Nothing left to ask

credentials: []
files.node.yaml:
type: TaskRunner

# A PROMISE NODE WITH A CONTINUE INPUT, which is not a contradiction and is exactly what
# LoopStart is. It settles once per pass; what re-fires it is the next set of answers arriving
# on `collected`, so each step of the task is a fresh execution of this node rather than one
# execution holding itself open. Declaring CallbackNode would make the engine drive it as an
# actor, and there is nothing here to keep alive between steps: the task's own paused row is
# the memory, which is what lets a dropped call be carried on tomorrow.
kind: PromiseNode

name: Task Runner
category: Flow
color: "#0ea5e9"
logoUrl: https://res.cloudinary.com/sonik/image/upload/v1751366180/gravity/icons/gravityIcon.png

description: Runs one task a step at a time, handing out what it still needs and taking back the answers

whenToUse: >-
  Carry a task that is waiting on a person through to the end: an application half filled in, a
  form left at a step, anything held open for someone with some of it already answered. Give it
  the task and what is already known, and it answers with the one step still outstanding and the
  fields that step asks for, takes the answers back, and says when nothing is left. Deciding
  WHICH task to do, and asking the questions out loud, are different jobs: this one only works
  out what is still needed and keeps count as it comes in. It walks the steps in the order the
  task declares them, so a later step is never handed out while an earlier one is short.

# WHO MAY RUN THIS (DECLARATIVE_NODES.md §9.13). Compulsory on every node.
#
# `required: false` adds no requirement of its own: the node runs for whoever the trigger
# admitted. It reaches nothing and decides nothing about a person, so there is nothing here to
# narrow.
auth:
  required: false

capabilities:
  # NOT cacheable. The whole point is to answer differently each time it is asked: a cached
  # first reply would hand out step one forever and the task would never move.
  cacheable: false
files.test.yaml:
# A REAL PAUSED TASK, created through the same route the platform uses, because the fixture
# runs the node's calls for real and there is no way to stand in for them.
#
# The task declares no steps, so the questions come from its own slice, which is what a
# component task's saved state IS: four fields answered and five empty, and an empty key is a
# question still outstanding.
#
# `national_idSource` is in that slice on purpose. Every proposed field on a SAB application
# carries a Source twin saying where the value came from, and asking someone for their
# "national id source" is nonsense, so this fails if a twin is ever offered as a question.
#
# `completeWhenDone` is off and fields are outstanding, so neither write fires: what is under
# test here is the reading and the arithmetic.

testData:
  config:
    runId: task_wf-vhmlce_1790006335623_73f886d
    completeWhenDone: false
  inputs:
    signal: {}
  expect:
    task: >-
      return output.task.fields.indexOf('national_id') === 0
        && output.task.fields.indexOf('national_idSource') === -1
        && output.task.outstandingCount === 5
        && output.task.held.first_name === 'Gavin'
